Patient Education

What is a Hernia?

A hernia occurs when an internal organ or tissue pushes through a weak spot in the surrounding muscle or connective tissue. Understanding hernias is the first step toward effective treatment.

Book Consultation Learn Causes

Understanding Hernias

Medical definition and key concepts

What Exactly is a Hernia?

A hernia develops when an internal organ, typically part of the intestine or abdominal tissue, protrudes through a weakened area in the surrounding muscle or fascia (the tough membrane that holds organs in place).

Think of it like a tube sock where a sock pushes through a hole in the fabric. The "sock" represents the organ or tissue, and the "hole" represents the weak spot in your abdominal wall.

How Do Hernias Develop?

The progression from weak area to visible bulge

1

Weakness Develops

Natural weakness in the abdominal wall exists due to anatomy, aging, or previous surgery. Some people are born with this weakness.

2

Pressure Increases

Activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, lifting, straining) create force against the weak area.

3

Tissue Pushes Through

Internal tissue, often intestine or fatty tissue, begins pushing through the weakened spot, creating a hernia sac.

4

Bulge Appears

Over time, the bulge becomes visible and palpable, especially when standing, coughing, or straining. It may reduce when lying down.

Abdominal Wall Anatomy

Types of Hernias

Where hernias can develop in the body

Inguinal Hernia

Most common type, occurring in the groin area where the inguinal canal is located. More frequent in men.

70% of all hernias

Femoral Hernia

Occurs below the groin crease through the femoral canal. More common in women, higher risk of complications.

Less common

Umbilical Hernia

Appears at or near the belly button. Common in infants and adults who are overweight or have had multiple pregnancies.

Common in adults

Incisional Hernia

Develops at the site of a previous surgical incision. Can occur months or years after surgery.

Post-surgery risk

Ventral Hernia

General term for hernias through the front abdominal wall. Includes epigastric and Spigelian hernias.

Front abdominal wall

Hiatal Hernia

Occurs when part of the stomach pushes through the diaphragm into the chest cavity. Causes acid reflux symptoms.

Internal hernia

Hernia Symptoms

Warning signs to watch for

Visible Bulge

A noticeable lump or swelling, especially when standing, coughing, or straining. May disappear when lying down.

Pain or Discomfort

Aching, burning, or sharp pain at the hernia site. Often worsens with physical activity, coughing, or bending.

Heaviness or Dragging Sensation

Feeling of heaviness in the abdomen or groin area, as if something is pulling down.

Weakness in Groin/Abdomen

Generalized weakness in the groin or abdominal area, especially after physical exertion.

Swelling that Grows

Progressive enlargement of the bulge over time, indicating the hernia is worsening.

Symptoms that Reduce

Bulge may push back in (reducible) or become more prominent throughout the day.

🤷‍♂️ FAQ

Frequently asked questions

No, hernias do not heal on their own. Once the abdominal wall is weakened and tissue has protruded, surgical repair is the only definitive treatment. Without surgery, hernias typically continue to grow and may lead to serious complications.

There is a genetic predisposition to hernias. If your parents or siblings have had hernias, your risk is higher. However, lifestyle factors and activities also play a significant role in whether a hernia develops.

A hernia typically presents as a visible or palpable bulge that may increase with coughing or straining. Muscle pain usually doesn't cause a bulge and is more localized to specific movements. If you notice a bulge, see a specialist for proper diagnosis.

Untreated hernias can lead to serious complications including incarceration (contents trapped), strangulation (blood supply cut off), and obstruction (blockage of intestine). These are medical emergencies requiring immediate surgery.

Light activities may be okay, but you should avoid heavy lifting and intense core exercises that increase intra-abdominal pressure. Consult with Dr. Kumar for personalized guidance on safe exercises while you await surgery.
